This is Cantá, in Roraima, in the Brazilian Amazon.
Rosa just pulled up her cassava.
And after every harvest, she asks the same question...
What do I plant next?
AgroDeal helps her answer it.
The name says deal, but it sells nothing.
It lets the farmer choose what to optimize.
First, the problem, measured with NASA POWER.
From June to September, Cantá got three hundred and thirty millimeters of rain.
The average is eight hundred and fifty-nine. The lowest since 1981.
The longest dry spell in the rainy season: twenty-four days. Normally, nine.
By September, the soil was as dry as in January. Five months early.
Will 2027 repeat it?
In El Niño years, that rain ranged from forty-eight percent below average, to seventeen above.
There is no rule. So we don't predict. We observe.
Second, the people.
In the last census, eighty-seven percent of Roraima's farms had no technical assistance.
Right now, the state extension agency tells families to choose crops suited to the dry period...
but it only reaches as far as an agent can drive.
In our survey, most families plant again right after harvest.
And a farmer in Goiás told us many were afraid to invest.
Tools exist.
Brazil's official zoning tells you when to plant the crop you already chose.
And a peer-reviewed study found that almost all rotation tools optimize only profit, for big farms.
None we found starts from the harvest, and lets the small farmer pick the goal.
So, back to Rosa.
Better soil? Cowpea. It's not related to cassava, so the pest left in the ground won't take it.
Low risk, in July? Cowpea again, for another reason. Out of the ground in seventy days.
July is inside the official cowpea window, so the fit jumps from fifty-three to eighty-seven percent.
Ask for pasture: brachiaria. But it admits it doesn't know how long it takes.
Ask about income: it says it can't measure that.
Every option gets three numbers. Never mixed.
Risk: from NASA rain and soil moisture, adjusted to this year.
Fit: from crop traits, weighed by her choice.
And confidence: how much we could actually measure.
Plain arithmetic on named data, in the browser. No model guesses a number.
Same maize, same code, two places.
Cantá, in April: six hundred and eighty-six millimeters, against five hundred needed. Low risk.
Rio Verde, in September: three hundred and eighty-six. High risk.
What it can't do, it says. No rain forecast. No prices. Fourteen crops, so far.
Next: more official windows, field tests in Roraima, and WhatsApp.
AgroDeal won't tell Rosa what to do.
It shows what each choice does to her soil, this year.
What do I plant next?
Now, she can explore it.
